st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The statement directly supports selective, human-led deployment: it treats current legal AI as assistive rather than a substitute for professional expertise, confines use to lower-risk and readily verifiable tasks, requires personal verification, and recommends risk-based policies and active supervision. Its emphasis is regulatory and operational rather than empirical, but it aligns closely with the cluster’s principal proposition.

kp.k: AI literacy is necessary for modern legal practice
kp.d: The regulators state that lawyers need to understand AI’s capabilities and limitations because lawyers, clients and third parties may use it. Clients may also require advice about lawful AI use or assistance after being adversely affected by AI.
qs: It is important for lawyers to understand AI, including the capabilities and limitations of the large language models (LLMs) and foundation models that underpin the latest AI tools — not only because lawyers may use AI themselves, but also because their clients may be using AI, seeking advice on how to lawfully use AI, or adversely affected by a third party’s use of AI.

kp.k: Existing professional obligations continue to govern AI use
kp.d: The statement does not create a separate AI-specific ethical regime; it directs lawyers using AI and other legal technology to maintain existing ethical standards and comply with the Uniform Law and applicable solicitors’ or barristers’ conduct rules.
qs: When using AI and other legal technology, lawyers must continue to maintain high ethical standards and comply with their professional obligations under the Legal Profession Uni- form Law (Uniform Law), and either the Legal Profession Uniform Law Australian Solicitors’ Conduct Rules 2015 (ASCR), or the Legal Profession Uniform Conduct (Barristers) Rules 2015 (BR)

kp.k: Public AI tools cannot safely receive client confidences
kp.d: Lawyers must not enter confidential, sensitive or privileged client information into public AI chatbots, copilots or other public tools. Before putting client information into a commercial AI product, they must examine its contractual terms to determine whether the information will remain secure.
qs: Lawyers cannot safely enter confidential, sensitive or privileged client information into public AI chatbots/co- pilots (like ChatGPT), or any other public tools.
If lawyers use commercial AI tools with any client information, they need to carefully review contractual terms to ensure the information will be kept secure.

kp.k: AI cannot replace independent forensic judgement
kp.d: The regulators characterise LLM-based tools as unable to reason, understand or advise. Lawyers remain personally responsible for assessing clients’ circumstances and exercising independent forensic judgement rather than treating AI output as legal advice or analysis.
qs: AI chatbots/ copilots and other LLM-based tools cannot reason, understand, or advise.

Lawyers are responsible for exercising their own forensic judgement when advising clients, and cannot rely on the output of an AI tool as a substitute for their own assessment and analysis of a client’s needs and circumstances.

kp.k: Lawyers must personally verify AI-generated legal content
kp.d: Current LLM tools are said to remain capable of hallucinations, defined here as fluent and convincing but inaccurate responses. Lawyers using AI to prepare documents must be qualified to verify the information, actually check its accuracy and ensure that it will not mislead clients, courts or other parties.
qs: AI chatbots/copilots, research assistants, and summarisers cannot be relied on as a substitute for legal knowledge, experi- ence or expertise.

No tool based on current LLMs can be free of ‘hallucinations’ (i.e. responses which are fluent and convincing, but inaccurate), and lawyers using AI to prepare documents must be able and qualified to personally verify the information they contain, and must actually ensure that their contents are accurate, and not likely to mislead their client, the court, or another party.

kp.k: AI-supported billing must reflect work actually performed
kp.d: AI use does not relax lawyers’ duties to charge fair, reasonable and proportionate costs. Bills must accurately represent work performed by law-practice staff, and AI should not raise client costs above traditional methods through avoidable verification or correction work.
qs: Lawyers using AI to support their work should ensure that the time and work items they bill clients for accurately represent the legal work done by law practice staff for their client.
Lawyers who use AI should ensure that it does not unnecessarily increase costs for their client above traditional methods (e.g. be- cause of additional time spent verifying or correcting its output).

kp.k: Practices should adopt clear risk-based AI policies
kp.d: The regulators recommend policies addressing approved tools, authorised users, permitted purposes, allowable information and measures to reduce data and security breaches. They also recommend making these policies available to clients on request to improve transparency.
qs: Implementing clear, risk-based policies to minimise data and security breach- es, and set out what AI tools they have decided to use in their practice, who can use those tools, for what purposes, and with what information.
We recommend that lawyers make these policies available to clients upon request to increase transparency (see below).

kp.k: Junior and support staff require continuous AI supervision
kp.d: Internal AI policies should provide for continuous, active supervision of junior and support staff. They should also establish review and verification processes for documents containing AI-generated material before those documents are settled.
qs: These policies should also set out how they will continuously and actively supervise the use of AI tools by junior and support staff, and how documents containing AI-generated content will be re- viewed for accuracy, and verified before they are settled.

kp.k: AI use should favour low-risk verifiable tasks
kp.d: The statement recommends restricting AI to lower-risk tasks that are easier to check, such as polite email drafting or suggestions for structuring an argument. It recommends prohibiting use for higher-risk tasks requiring independent verification, including translation of advice, analysis of unfamiliar legal concepts and executive decision-making.
qs: Limiting the use of AI tools in their practice to tasks which are lower-risk and easier to verify (e.g. drafting a polite email or suggesting how to structure an argument) and prohibiting its use for tasks which are higher-risk and which should be independently verified (e.g. translating advice into another language, analysing an unfamiliar legal concept or executive decision-making).

kp.k: Bias and human factors constrain appropriate AI use
kp.d: The regulators warn that generative AI can be biased and cannot understand human psychology or external complicating factors. These limitations may make it unsuitable where legal work depends on contextual or human assessment.
qs: Generative AI tools can be biased, and can- not understand human psychology or other external complicating factors that may be relevant.

kp.k: Training data may create serious ethical concerns
kp.d: Lawyers are advised to consider intellectual-property and ownership issues in AI training data, as well as the possible inclusion of offensive or unlawful material, including child exploitation material. Such concerns may make a model inappropriate for legal work.
qs: There may also be ethical concerns with the training data used for an AI model, including intellectual property and ownership rights, or the inclusion of highly offensive or unlawful text or imagery (including child exploitation material) that may make them inappropriate to use in your work.

kp.k: AI use and cost effects should be transparent
kp.d: Lawyers should record and disclose when and how AI was used in a matter, including how its use affected costs, to clients and, where necessary or appropriate, courts and other practitioners. They should proactively address ethical concerns raised by clients.
qs: Being transparent about their use of AI, and properly recording and disclosing to their clients (and where necessary or appropriate, the court and fellow practitioners) when and how they have used AI in a matter and how the use of AI is reflected in costs, if requested by the client
Lawyers should carefully consider any ethical concerns about the use of AI raised by their clients, and address them proactively.

kp.k: Regulatory AI guidance will evolve over time
kp.d: The issuing regulators describe the statement as guidance on their expectations rather than a final account of AI practice, and undertake to review and update it as professional use of AI develops.
qs: We will regularly review and update our guidance on AI for lawyers, as its use in the legal profession continues to evolve.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The joint regulators describe AI as an assistive technology that introduces confidentiality, accuracy, supervision and billing risks without replacing lawyers’ independent judgment or professional responsibilities.
pts.d: The Law Society of New South Wales, the Legal Practice Board of Western Australia and the Victorian Legal Services Board + Commissioner state that lawyers need to understand AI both for their own practice and because clients may use it, seek advice on lawful use, or suffer adverse effects from third-party use. They assert that LLM-based tools cannot reason, understand or advise and cannot replace legal expertise; current LLMs cannot be free of hallucinations. Lawyers must therefore independently assess clients’ circumstances and personally verify AI-assisted documents. The regulators say confidential client information cannot safely be entered into public AI tools, while commercial tools require contractual security review. They also identify possible bias, limitations in understanding human circumstances, and ethical concerns about training data. Their recommendations favour lower-risk, readily verifiable uses, risk-based practice policies, active supervision of junior and support staff, and transparency with clients. They warn that verification and correction can increase costs rather than necessarily deliver savings: billing should reflect work actually performed by practice staff and should not unnecessarily exceed traditional-method costs. These are present-tense claims and regulatory expectations, not forecasts of employment displacement or market restructuring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The statement relies on regulatory authority and existing professional obligations, not empirical evaluations of AI performance or economic effects.
pts.d: The three issuing bodies frame the document as their expectations for lawyers using AI. They cite the Legal Profession Uniform Law and the Australian Solicitors’ Conduct Rules or Barristers’ Rules: confidentiality (ASCR r 9.1; BR r 114), independent advice (ASCR r 4.1.4; BR rr 3(b), 4(e) and 42), honesty, competence and diligence (ASCR rr 4.1.2 and 4.1.3; BR rr 4(c)–(d), 8(a) and 35), and fair, reasonable and proportionate costs (Uniform Law ss 172–173; ASCR r 12.2). Those authorities ground the professional duties. The statement supplies no datasets, benchmark results, measured hallucination rates, named court incidents or cost studies to support its technological and economic risk claims. Its task examples illustrate recommended risk distinctions rather than report observed outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The guidance concerns current AI use as of the 2024 statement, with no dated forecast; expectations depend on the tool, information, task risk and ability to verify output.
pts.d: The claim about unavoidable hallucinations expressly concerns current LLMs, and the regulators commit to reviewing guidance as professional use evolves. Public tools and commercial tools receive different confidentiality treatment: the former are deemed unsafe for confidential, sensitive or privileged client information, while the latter require careful contractual review when used with client information. The statement distinguishes mandatory continuing professional duties from recommendations that lawyers should consider. It recommends limiting AI to lower-risk, easier-to-verify tasks and prohibiting higher-risk uses such as translating advice, analysing unfamiliar legal concepts or executive decision-making. Lawyers preparing documents with AI must both be qualified to verify their contents and actually ensure accuracy. Disclosure to courts and fellow practitioners is qualified by necessity or appropriateness, and the text links disclosure about use and costs to client requests.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are practising lawyers, junior and support staff, clients, courts and other parties; no particular firm size or legal-market segment is singled out.
pts.d: Lawyers retain responsibility for judgment, confidentiality, verification, billing and supervision even when using AI. Junior and support staff are expressly subject to continuous, active supervision under recommended practice policies. Clients face possible information exposure, inaccurate advice or documents, training-data ethical concerns, and additional verification or correction costs; the guidance calls for transparency and attention to clients’ concerns. Courts, fellow practitioners and other parties may encounter AI-generated material, so lawyers must ensure documents are accurate and not misleading and disclose AI use where necessary or appropriate. Clients are also affected outside the lawyer’s workflow through their own AI use and third parties’ use, creating a need for AI-related legal understanding and advice. Although the introduction mentions the profession’s access-to-justice role, the statement makes no concrete prediction that AI will reduce unmet legal need.
